source.title: Why Warmup the Learning Rate? Underlying Mechanisms and Improvements

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether training can recover after learning-rate instabilities using a different setup from the claim version: FCNs on CIFAR-10 with MSE loss, with sharpness and loss trajectories.
record.gate_note: The paper's main experiments concern warmup and sharpness, not training classification error. Results cited from prior work are not rows. The relevant evidence is the paper's own FCN loss and sharpness trajectories in Figure 1 and the accompanying description of instability and recovery.
record.test_reason: The study measures training loss and Hessian sharpness during GD training with squared loss, directly bearing on V5's instability, sharpness reduction and recovery mechanism. It varies warmup schedules rather than reproducing the original constant-rate experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the conclusion. More precisely, warmup primarily permits larger target learning rates by reducing sharpness, or preconditioned sharpness for Adam, through natural evolution and/or self-stabilization. At fixed target rate, longer warmup usually adds only marginal benefit away from failure boundaries. Excessive instabilities can cause SGD divergence or Adam training failure; sufficiently moderate instabilities can resolve.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GD on FCNs trained on a CIFAR-10 subset with MSE loss and varies linear warmup duration; the cited learning-rate version also concerns instability recovery but specifies wide networks and low training loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on initialization/parameterization (SP versus µP), target learning rate, and warmup duration. The paper describes distinct sharpness-reduction and progressive-sharpening regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam's instability tracks preconditioned sharpness, and severe early catapults can leave finite but high loss and halted training rather than unbounded divergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive optimizers have optimizer-specific stability thresholds and can fail through persistent high-loss states after early instabilities.

fits_no_version.finding: SP versus µP and warmup duration change natural sharpness evolution and the maximum trainable target learning rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameterization and warmup jointly determine learning-rate tolerance through sharpness dynamics.

record.problems: The relevant training-loss trajectories are figure-only, without numerical endpoints or error bars. The paper reports that phase diagrams lack error bars because of computational cost. The tested setup is limited to a 5k CIFAR-10 subset, FCNs, MSE loss, and GD; it does not report classification training error.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Figure 1 also shows µP trajectories at target rate 1/λH0, but that target is not the above-initial-stability condition named by V5. Other figures and phase diagrams report test performance or optimizer comparisons rather than the V5 training-loss outcome.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error under the stated successful training recipes, random-label memorization, and model-size or early-stopping comparisons.
Teacher-student local minima and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth, matched identity-shortcut comparisons, and the special-initialization exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization effects on training speed and trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian weights or convolution kernels.

A readable low final training-loss endpoint for the recorded GD recovery trajectory; width scaling; a constant-rate recovery interval just above the initial stability limit; and divergence despite starting below that limit. The recorded warmup runs also do not establish prolonged constant-rate edge-of-stability behavior.
Matched batch-normalized versus unnormalized training and Fixup comparisons. The WRNs use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source. R1's divergence does not itself limit V5, which already predicts divergence at sufficiently large rates. The declared omission of Figure 1's µP trajectories is poorly justified: V5 also includes progressive sharpening toward the stability threshold, so a target below the initial threshold does not make those trajectories irrelevant. Their persistent threshold-tracking during warmup is described in Section 4.1, but prolonged constant-rate behavior remains unestablished. No individual curve endpoints can be recovered reliably from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and comparisons by model size or training duration.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual networks as a function of depth, and the stated special-initialization or normalization comparisons.
Whether activation-matched initializations improve learning speed or trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization comparisons.

The tested result uses FCNs on a 5k CIFAR-10 subset with MSE loss and GD; it does not establish behavior across wide-network scaling, other learning-rate ranges, or full-batch training over longer times. The Cohen et al. and Gilmer et al. cases named in the version are not tested here.
Batch normalization comparisons and Fixup residual-network training without normalization.

rows.subject: FCN-4-512 in SP
rows.operation_detail: Trained with GD using MSE loss and a linear warmup schedule.
rows.measure: Training loss trajectory; the accompanying text describes whether instability resolves or leads to divergence.
rows.note: The paper states that failure to reduce sharpness over extended steps may result in training divergence, citing the Twrm = 1 case in this figure. It does not report a numerical endpoint.
rows.check: Section 3 explicitly identifies this trajectory as divergence. Divergence at an excessive learning rate is a predicted part of V5, so 'absent' incorrectly treats every failure to recover as contrary evidence. Twrm = 1 means constant-rate training; the target is 16 times the initial linearized stability limit.
